# Checking a Collection

:::{.callout-note title="Partly written"}
First draft, 2026-10-21. Reads `co021` and `wa082` from the files in `data/`. Every number in the text is computed when the book builds. Filling the 1900 gap moved to 08 Detrending on 2026-10-19. Open questions are in the backlog.
:::

## Big Idea

You have a collection read into R. Before you date anything, what do you actually have? How many series, how long, how deep in each century, and is anything in the file going to break the analysis later? None of this is glamorous. It is the part of the work where you find out that one core has a hole in it, or that the early centuries rest on a handful of trees, while it is still cheap to find out.

The two collections answer these questions very differently, which is why they make a good pair. Mesa Verde is long, deep, and full of absent rings. Hurricane Ridge is short, with no absent rings and one year nobody measured.

## Packages

```{r}
#| label: check-setup
#| message: false
library(dplR)
library(ggplot2)
co021 <- read.rwl("data/co021.rwl", format = "tucson")
wa082 <- read.rwl("data/wa082.rwl", format = "tucson")
```

These are the files from the previous chapter, read the same way. That matters for `wa082`. The on-board copy holds a zero in 1900 where the file has no measurement, and this chapter is partly about that gap.

## Checking Mesa Verde

`rwl.check` does two jobs. It describes a collection, and it reads through it looking for anything that will cause trouble later.

```{r}
#| label: check-rwlcheck-co021
co021Check <- rwl.check(co021)
co021Check
```

```{r}
#| label: check-rwlcheck-co021-numbers
#| include: false
co021Findings <- as.data.frame(co021Check)
coRuns <- co021Findings[co021Findings$check == "RWL_CONSECUTIVE_ZERO", ]
```

The top of the printout is the description. Mesa Verde's file has no header, so there is no site name or species to show, only the precision. The series average `r round(co021Check$meta$mean.length)` rings. The mean lag-one autocorrelation comes back in the next section. The last line of the description says the most. It is each series' correlation with a master built from all the other series, after a 32-year spline takes out the slow trend. At Mesa Verde that averages `r round(co021Check$meta$mean.cor, 2)`, with a standard deviation of `r round(co021Check$meta$sd.cor, 2)`, so every series agrees with the rest, and about equally well.

Below the description are the findings. `rwl.check` runs `r nrow(rwl.check.catalogue())` checks in `r length(unique(rwl.check.catalogue()$group))` groups, and `rwl.check.catalogue()` lists them all with a line on each. Every finding has a severity. An error means the data can't be right as they stand: two series with identical measurements, a year in the future, a series that looks a year or more off. A warning means something will change a result or stop a function, and you have to decide what to do about it. A note is something you should know.

Mesa Verde has no errors and no warnings. The `r nrow(co021Findings)` notes are of three kinds. `RWL_LOW_DEPTH` says the years before 1200 rest on fewer than two series, which is one core, 646118, on its own. `RWL_ZERO_RING` counts the absent rings: `r sum(co021 == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of them, `r round(100 * mean(co021 == 0, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` percent of all the measurements. `RWL_CONSECUTIVE_ZERO` lists every place a series is missing more than one ring in a row, `r nrow(coRuns)` of them. The printout shows the first ten, and `as.data.frame(co021Check)` gives all of them as a table, one row per finding.

Look at where the absent rings fall and some years keep coming back. In 1585, `r sum(co021["1585", ] == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r sum(!is.na(co021["1585", ]))` series have no ring at all, and `r sum(co021["1584", ] == 0 & co021["1585", ] == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` of them are missing both 1584 and 1585. So what does a note ask of you? To know it. Absent rings that line up across trees are dating evidence, and the crossdating chapters use them. The longest run at Mesa Verde is `r max(coRuns$n)` rings. Ten or more in a row would be a warning, `RWL_ZERO_RUN`, because a run that long is more likely a gap somebody filled with zeros than years the tree grew no ring at that core.

Is `r round(100 * mean(co021 == 0, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` percent a lot? St. George and colleagues counted the absent rings in 2,359 Northern Hemisphere ring-width records from the ITRDB [@StGeorge2013]. Over all of them there was one absent ring for every 240 present, and 0.6 percent of Douglas-fir rings were absent. Mesa Verde has one for every `r round(sum(co021 > 0, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(co021 == 0, na.rm = TRUE))`. More than half of their records had no absent rings at all, and the ones with more than 2 percent were all in the American Southwest. Where many records in the Southwest lost a ring in the same year, the year was a severe drought. I haven't checked Mesa Verde's absent years against a drought record, so that's as far as I'll go here.

## Checking Hurricane Ridge

```{r}
#| label: check-rwlcheck-wa082
wa082Check <- rwl.check(wa082)
wa082Check
```

This file has a header, and the description reads it: the site, the species, the elevation and location as the file writes them, and who collected the cores. The series average `r round(wa082Check$meta$mean.length)` rings, about a third of Mesa Verde's. The mean correlation with the master is `r round(wa082Check$meta$mean.cor, 2)`, against `r round(co021Check$meta$mean.cor, 2)` at Mesa Verde. That is the gap between a collection where everything agrees and an ordinary one. [Data Sources](A2DataSources.qmd) ranks both against the rest of the ITRDB on a close cousin of this number, the interseries correlation from `xdate.report`.

That correlation is over `r wa082Check$meta$n.cor` of the `r wa082Check$meta$n.series` series, and the findings say why. One warning and one note, both about 712011. Read the warning through. It says the gap is not a fault in the file, names the five functions that will fail on it, and says how to close it. The note follows from the warning. The master correlation and the crossdating checks behind it need each series splined first, and a series with a hole in it can't be splined. So 712011 wasn't checked at all, and the clean result for the other series says nothing about it.

The crossdating checks also look for a better correlation at a lag of up to five years, and every other series at both sites passed. That is a first look at the whole series, and the crossdating chapters do the job properly, segment by segment. It is also the slow part of `rwl.check`; `checks` lets you leave it out when you are sweeping through many files.

## Series Statistics

`summary` on a `rwl` object calls `rwl.stats` and returns one row per series.

```{r}
#| label: check-stats
co021Stats <- summary(co021)
wa082Stats <- summary(wa082)
head(wa082Stats)
```

Mean, median, standard deviation, skew and kurtosis are what they always are. Two columns are more particular to tree rings. `ar1` is the lag-one autocorrelation, how much a ring resembles the one before it. `gini` is the Gini coefficient, a measure of how unequal the rings in a series are, which Biondi and Qeadan proposed as a replacement for mean sensitivity. The arithmetic is the one economists use on incomes.

`ar1` is the column I look at first, because it tells you how much memory the trees carry from one year to the next, and that memory is what prewhitening removes before crossdating.

```{r}
#| label: check-ar1
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Lag-one autocorrelation of each series in the two collections."
ar1 <- data.frame(
  site = rep(c("co021", "wa082"), c(nrow(co021Stats), nrow(wa082Stats))),
  ar1 = c(co021Stats$ar1, wa082Stats$ar1)
)
ggplot(ar1, aes(x = site, y = ar1)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.3, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = expression(phi[1])) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Both collections carry a lot of memory, Hurricane Ridge more on average (median `r round(median(wa082Stats$ar1), 2)` against `r round(median(co021Stats$ar1), 2)`). Some of that is the age trend. A series that declines slowly over two centuries is autocorrelated whether or not the tree remembers anything, so this is memory and trend together. Detrending separates them.

:::{.callout-note title="For Andy"}
The Gini sentence cites Biondi and Qeadan (2008) from memory of the dplR help page. The paper is not in `dplR.bib` yet. Check the claim and add the entry, or cut the attribution.
:::

## Seeing the Collection

`summary` gives each series' first and last year. A segment plot draws them.

```{r}
#| label: check-seg-co021
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "The span of each series in `co021`, sorted by first year."
plot(co021, plot.type = "seg")
```

One bar per series, sorted by the year it starts. The staircase is the collection getting deeper as you come forward in time. The oldest series, 646118, starts in `r co021Stats$first[co021Stats$series == "646118"]` and stops in `r co021Stats$last[co021Stats$series == "646118"]`, and for its first `r min(co021Stats$first[co021Stats$series != "646118"]) - min(co021Stats$first)` years it is the only series there is. Two others stop early too: 645232 in `r co021Stats$last[co021Stats$series == "645232"]` and 646107 in `r co021Stats$last[co021Stats$series == "646107"]`. The other `r sum(co021Stats$last >= 1962)` run to `r max(co021Stats$last) - 1` or `r max(co021Stats$last)`. Is a bar that stops in 1400 a problem? Not by itself. The core might come from a snag, or the measurable wood might end at a rot pocket, and only the field notes can say which. The plot tells you which cores to ask about.

```{r}
#| label: check-seg-wa082
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "The span of each series in `wa082`, sorted by first year."
plot(wa082, plot.type = "seg")
```

Hurricane Ridge is a shorter staircase. Its last series to start, 712072, begins in `r max(wa082Stats$first)`, `r max(wa082Stats$first) - min(wa082Stats$first)` years after the first. One series, `r wa082Stats$series[wa082Stats$last < 1983]`, stops in `r min(wa082Stats$last)`, and the rest run to 1983. Where is the gap in 712011? At this scale a single year doesn't show. `rwl.check` told you about 1900, and this plot never would have. Watch for it in the next figure.

Count the series in each year and you have sample depth, the staircase turned into a number.

```{r}
#| label: check-depth
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Sample depth, the number of series measured in each year."
depth <- data.frame(
  site = rep(c("co021", "wa082"), c(nrow(co021), nrow(wa082))),
  year = c(time(co021), time(wa082)),
  n = c(rowSums(!is.na(co021)), rowSums(!is.na(wa082)))
)
ggplot(depth, aes(x = year, y = n, linetype = site)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Number of series", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: check-depth-numbers
#| include: false
coDepth <- depth[depth$site == "co021", ]
waDepth <- depth[depth$site == "wa082", ]
firstWith <- function(d, k) min(d$year[d$n >= k])
```

Mesa Verde has 5 series by `r firstWith(coDepth, 5)` and 10 by `r firstWith(coDepth, 10)`. It peaks at `r max(coDepth$n)` series from `r min(coDepth$year[coDepth$n == max(coDepth$n)])` to `r max(coDepth$year[coDepth$n == max(coDepth$n)])`, and it never has all `r ncol(co021)` at once, because 646118 had stopped long before the youngest series began. Hurricane Ridge has 10 series by `r firstWith(waDepth, 10)`, and all `r ncol(wa082)` only from `r min(waDepth$year[waDepth$n == ncol(wa082)])` to `r max(waDepth$year[waDepth$n == ncol(wa082)])`, except in 1900, when it has `r waDepth$n[waDepth$year == 1900]`. That one-year notch in the dashed line is 712011's gap. Sample depth counts measurements, so a year nobody measured comes off the count.

How many series is enough? That depends on how well they agree, which is why there is no single number. [Chronology Statistics](09ChronologyStats.qmd) works it out with the subsample signal strength, and [Chronology Building](10Chronologies.qmd) uses that to decide where a chronology should start. For now the figure says where the record is thin: the thirteenth century at Mesa Verde and most of the eighteenth at Hurricane Ridge.

There is one more of `dplR`'s plots to meet, the spaghetti plot.

```{r}
#| label: check-spag
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Every series in `co021`, each on its own baseline."
plot(co021, plot.type = "spag")
```

Every series, each drawn on its own baseline. Nobody crossdates from this. At 35 series and nearly 800 years the year-to-year detail is a blur. One thing does show: many series start wide and narrow as they go. `r round(100 * mean(sapply(co021, function(s) { s <- s[!is.na(s)]; mean(s[1:30]) > mean(s[-(1:30)]) })))` percent of Mesa Verde's series have wider rings in their first 30 years than in the rest, and `r round(100 * mean(sapply(wa082, function(s) { s <- s[!is.na(s)]; mean(s[1:30]) > mean(s[-(1:30)]) })))` percent at Hurricane Ridge. That is the age trend, and [Detrending](08Detrending.qmd) is about taking it out. I look at a spaghetti plot once and move on.

## The Gap in 712011

So what do you do about 712011? For now, nothing. The gap stays open through crossdating, on purpose. Every fill borrows its value from somewhere. A zero claims the tree grew no ring, and the fills in `fill.internal.NA` borrow from the series' own neighbours or from the other trees. A value borrowed from the other trees agrees with them by construction, and a dating check that a series passes because you wrote part of the answer into it is no check at all. `xdate.report` leaves 712011 out and says why, and `corr.rwl.seg` skips the segments that include 1900. The crossdating chapters run on `co021`, so little is lost. The first function that refuses the gap outright is `detrend`, so the fill comes at the start of [Detrending](08Detrending.qmd).

## Trimming

Sometimes you want less of a collection: one stretch of years, or a few of the series. `window` cuts a collection to a span.

```{r}
#| label: check-window
#| message: true
co021Recent <- window(co021, start = 1900, end = 1950)
dim(co021Recent)
```

Two series have no rings between 1900 and 1950, and `window` drops them and names them. That leaves `r ncol(co021Recent)` series over `r nrow(co021Recent)` years. Why drop them? A column with nothing in it is a trap for later. Some functions skip it, and some stop with a message that doesn't point anywhere near the cause.

`subset` picks series. Here are the two cores from tree 1 at Hurricane Ridge.

```{r}
#| label: check-subset
wa082Tree1 <- subset(wa082, select = c("712011", "712012"))
class(wa082Tree1)
range(time(wa082Tree1))
```

The result is still class `rwl`, and the years shrink to fit the series you kept. Tree 1's older core starts in `r min(time(wa082Tree1))`, so the years before that are gone.

Square brackets work too, since an `rwl` object is a data frame underneath, and they behave differently on purpose.

```{r}
#| label: check-bracket
#| error: true
co021Early <- co021[time(co021) <= 1300, ]
sum(colSums(!is.na(co021Early)) == 0)
summary(co021Early)
```

`[` keeps all `r ncol(co021Early)` columns, `r sum(colSums(!is.na(co021Early)) == 0)` of them empty, so that `x[i, j]` always gives back the columns `j` names and stays lined up with anything else indexed the same way, like a table of tree IDs. And then `summary` stops with a message about a `ts` object. That's the trap. If you index with brackets, the empty columns are yours to clean up. Use `window` and `subset` and they're taken care of. The [aside on classes and generics](04xAsideClassesGenerics.qmd) says more about why an `rwl` object behaves like a data frame most of the time and not all of it.

## Wrapping Up

None of these checks tells you whether the rings are dated correctly. Shift part of a series by a year and its mean, its autocorrelation and its segment length barely move. That takes crossdating, the subject of the next chapter, [Crossdating a Collection](05Crossdating.qmd). In a project, it comes before you detrend anything.

## Exercises

- Which `co021` series has the most absent rings, and what fraction of its length is that? Does it come from a tree whose other cores also have many?
- Make a table of the years in which more than half of the `co021` series present have a zero. How many are there?
- Run `xdate.report` on `wa082` and find 712011 in what it returns. What does it say, and what are your three ways forward?

## Further Reading

- @Wigley1984 is the paper behind "how many series is enough?" Their Figure 2 is a sample-depth plot much like the one in this chapter, for three English chronologies, and pages 206 and 207 work out how far back each one still stands in for the full collection. The answer runs from 4 cores at one site to 8 at another, depending on how well the cores agree, and they offer their 0.85 cutoff "only as a guide". [Chronology Statistics](09ChronologyStats.qmd) takes it up properly.
- @StGeorge2013 is five pages on where absent rings turn up across the Northern Hemisphere, by genus, latitude and year. They counted the zeros in 2,359 files, after checking that it made no difference to count measurements of 0.001 mm as well, for investigators who mark an absent ring with the smallest value the format allows.
- To add: Biondi and Qeadan (2008) on the Gini coefficient, once checked.
- The `rwl.check` help page describes every check and the control values that tune them, including why the crossdating checks compare a series with its own collection instead of a fixed correlation.
